growth_story.headline: After war and a long post-2008 slump, Croatia's growth sped up to 4.3 percent a year from 2016, lifted lately by EU money and spending, and is now cooling.
growth_story.arc: In 1991-1999 income per person shrank by 1.0 percent a year on average: war and a hard transition from socialism cut it by 19.6 percent in 1991 alone, and prices rose 1,500 percent in 1993. From 2000 to 2007 growth averaged 5.1 percent a year, but the World Bank says this boom ran on spending at home and plentiful money from abroad rather than on exports. When the 2008 global crisis cut off that money, a six-year recession followed: income per person fell 6.7 percent in 2009, and growth averaged -0.4 percent over 2008-2015. Since 2016 growth has averaged 4.3 percent a year, up from 0.7 in the decade before; the pandemic cut income per person by 7.5 percent in 2020 before a 13.7 percent rebound in 2021, and since then rising wages, public spending and EU funds have lifted demand. Income per person reached a new high in 2025, but growth has eased since the rebound, to 3.1 percent in 2025.

since_last_year.text: Growth has kept slowing. Income per person grew 3.1 percent in 2025, down from 3.7 in 2024. The World Bank's October 2026 update says growth slowed further in the first half of 2026, as household spending and EU-funded investment grew more slowly, tourism stalled and fewer work permits went to foreign workers.

citations.quote: slower annual employment growth and decline in the number of work permits issued to foreign workers point to weakening labor demand

growth_story.tension: The World Bank says Croatia's catch-up with average EU incomes has stalled since 2023. In the data, though, income per person kept rising, from 17,225 dollars in 2023 to a new high of 18,414 in 2025, and the OECD, writing in January 2026, says catch-up toward average OECD living standards continues. Both can be true if the rest of the EU grew about as fast, and the two sources compare Croatia with different groups. The sources and the data also measure the 2008-2015 slump differently: the World Bank describes a six-year recession in the whole economy, while income per person fell less, perhaps partly because many people emigrated.
